analysis.investment_thesis: Avanti Feeds is the dominant Indian shrimp feed manufacturer with a pristine balance sheet (effectively zero debt, ROCE of 24%), but its commodity-adjacent, cyclical business model and a P/E of 31.7x on what appears to be a peak earnings year (₹557 Cr net profit) offers insufficient margin of safety for a Munger-style concentrated bet.
key_strengths: Market leadership in Indian shrimp feed with scale/distribution advantages over regional competitors
Fortress balance sheet: near-zero debt (₹15 Cr borrowings vs ₹3,011 Cr equity), enabling resilience through shrimp-cycle downturns
ROCE of 24% and net profit CAGR of 15% over 9 years demonstrate real capital efficiency above cost of capital
key_risks: Earnings are highly cyclical — operating income swung from ₹684 Cr (2018) down to ₹314 Cr (2022), exposing the market to severe mean-reversion risk at current valuations
Thin operating margins (~11.6%) leave little buffer against raw material spikes (fish meal, soybean), which are globally priced commodities
Other income of ₹166 Cr (30% of net profit) is inflating headline earnings — stripping it out reveals core business margins significantly weaker than they appear
red_flags: 2025 is likely a cyclical peak: EBITDA at ₹738 Cr is the highest ever, making the 31.7x P/E on peak earnings particularly dangerous — normalized P/E is closer to 45-50x
FCF/Net Income at 78% (₹437/₹557 Cr) is slightly below the 80% quality threshold; investing CF of -₹485 Cr in 2025 signals heavy capital deployment whose returns are unproven
Revenue growth has essentially stalled in the core 5-year period (2021: ₹4,101 Cr → 2025: ₹5,612 Cr = ~6.5% CAGR), undermining the growth premium embedded in the valuation
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Avanti Feeds passes the basic quality checklist — clean balance sheet, decent ROCE, understandable business — but as I always say, invert first. The shrimp feed business is structurally thin-margined and cyclical. The 2018 EBITDA peak of ₹708 Cr was followed by a brutal trough of ₹346 Cr in 2022 — a 51% collapse. The current ₹738 Cr EBITDA in 2025 looks suspiciously like another peak. At EV/EBITDA of 21x, the market is pricing this as if the cycle has been abolished. It hasn't.

The other income line deserves particular scrutiny: ₹166 Cr in FY25 (up from ₹54 Cr in FY22), driven by treasury/investment returns on accumulated cash, is papering over the core operating reality. A business where 30% of net profit comes from financial investments is telling you something. At 31.7x P/E on peak-cycle numbers, the stock offers a fair business at an unfair price — the precise inverse of what Munger seeks. I would wait for a cyclical trough that brings the price to 18-20x normalized earnings before considering a position.
